title: Dadu-Corki: Algorithm-Architecture Co-Design for Embodied AI-powered Robotic Manipulation
problem: Embodied AI robotic manipulation systems run LLM inference on a frame-by-frame basis, creating cumulative sequential latencies (LLM inference, robot control, data communication) that reach 249 ms per frame and prevent real-time operation at >=30 Hz. LLM inference alone consumes 72.7% of latency and 95.8% of energy per frame.
method: Corki decouples LLM inference from robot control by replacing per-frame discrete action prediction with cubic polynomial trajectory prediction over multiple future steps, reducing LLM inference frequency by up to 5.1x. A custom dataflow ASIC accelerator implements task-space computed torque control (TS-CTC) with pipelined link-level computations (pose, velocity, acceleration, force units connected via FIFOs and line buffers) and an application-specific approximate computing unit that skips matrix recomputation when joint angular movement is below a threshold (saving >51% of matrix updates). Communication latency is hidden by pipelining image capture and transmission concurrent with trajectory execution.

title: Micro Blossom: Accelerated Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching Decoding for Quantum Error Correction
problem: Minimum-Weight Perfect Matching (MWPM) decoders for quantum error correction (QEC) on surface codes require sub-microsecond latency to avoid accumulating idle logical errors during fault-tolerant gate feedforward, but all prior exact MWPM implementations on CPUs achieve multi-microsecond latency and the blossom algorithm was believed to be too complex for hardware acceleration. Approximate decoders that achieve low latency sacrifice accuracy, causing 1.7x-13.9x more logical errors at code distance 13.
method: Micro Blossom employs a heterogeneous CPU+FPGA architecture that partitions the blossom algorithm into primal (CPU) and dual (hardware) phases. The FPGA accelerator instantiates one vertex processing unit (vPU) and one edge processing unit (ePU) per node and edge in the decoding graph, achieving O(d^3) parallel PUs. The dual phase—the dominant bottleneck—is fully parallelized: each vPU maintains compact per-vertex state (residue, unique-touch, unique-node, direction) and communicates only with graph neighbors via a broadcast/convergecast network. Isolated conflicts (the common case at low error rates) are detected and resolved entirely in hardware without CPU involvement via parallel ePU logic, reducing average CPU interactions from O(p*|V|+1) to O(p^2*|V|+1). Round-wise fusion processes each measurement round incrementally as it arrives, achieving stream decoding with constant latency independent of the number of rounds. The hardware is generated from a decoding-graph JSON specification via SpinalHDL to synthesizable Verilog.

title: MEADOW: Memory Efficient Adaptable Dataflow for On-Device LLM Workloads
problem: Running LLM inference on edge FPGAs is severely constrained by the FPGA's limited on-chip SRAM and external DRAM bandwidth, making naive GEMM-based attention execution impractical at the bandwidth envelope of sub-10W devices.
method: Token-Parallel Head-Sequential (TPHS) dataflow partitions attention across token dimension in parallel while sequencing across heads to fit SRAM; weight packing extracts unique chunks from weight tensors, applies packet-specific encoding precision, and uses frequency-aware reindexing to minimize DRAM traffic. W8A8 quantization applied throughout.

title: Graph Learning at Scale: Characterizing and Optimizing Pre-Propagation GNNs
problem: Pre-propagation GNNs (PP-GNNs), which decouple feature propagation from training as a preprocessing step, suffer from data loading as their dominant bottleneck (88-91% of training time) and face severe scalability challenges from input expansion (K(R+1)x larger inputs).
method: The paper characterizes PP-GNN bottlenecks and proposes: (1) Chunk reshuffling that performs coarser shuffling enabling GPU-side batch assembly to replace fine-grained row-level shuffling; (2) Double-buffer prefetching to overlap I/O with computation; (3) GPU Direct Storage (GDS) for graphs exceeding host memory; (4) Tailored training strategies (mini-batch GD and chunk-based sampling) to handle input expansion. These optimizations target the I/O path from SSD/storage to GPU.

title: OmniSim: Simulating Hardware with C Speed and RTL Accuracy for High-Level Synthesis Designs
problem: High-Level Synthesis (HLS) tools cannot correctly simulate complex dataflow designs at the C level—particularly those with non-blocking FIFO accesses (read_nb/write_nb), infinite loops, and cyclic module dependencies—because the OS-level scheduling of software threads does not correspond to hardware timing, leading to incorrect functional results and inaccurate cycle counts; falling back to C/RTL co-simulation takes hours to days.
method: OmniSim introduces a multi-threaded simulation framework operating at the LLVM IR level. It classifies dataflow designs into three types (A: blocking-only/acyclic; B: non-blocking or cyclic but single-behavior; C: non-blocking with behavior depending on FIFO access outcome) and applies different simulation strategies accordingly. Key mechanisms: (1) one software thread per active dataflow module (Func Sim threads) plus a dedicated Performance Simulation thread (Perf Sim thread); (2) FIFO read/write timing tables that explicitly record the hardware cycle at which each FIFO event occurs, independent of OS thread scheduling; (3) a Query Pool where Func Sim threads pause on non-blocking FIFO accesses until the Perf Sim thread resolves the query by comparing hardware-cycle timestamps; (4) flexibly overlapped execution where Func Sim and Perf Sim threads run concurrently rather than in strict phases, yielding additional speedup. An LLVM pass instruments the IR to track basic block execution traces and rewrites dataflow functions to launch concurrent threads. Incremental simulation is supported to avoid full restarts when FIFO sizes change.
